If the oldest job is blocked by a newer job, the system becomes inefficient and unpredictable. This limitation makes FIFO less suitable for highly competitive environments where waiting time is unacceptable.

When compared to other policies, FIFO is generally preferred for its simplicity and predictable behavior. FIFO scheduling is a first-in-first-out algorithm that processes jobs based on their arrival order. It ensures that the oldest job in the queue is executed immediately, guaranteeing fair treatment for all arriving processes regardless of their relative timing. This simple rule creates a predictable and stable system where the earliest entry is always served first.

The core operation involves maintaining a queue where the head of the line holds the most recent job. When a process arrives, it is added to the front of this queue, and the oldest job is removed and executed next. This structure prevents any single job from dominating the system by ensuring no process blocks others indefinitely.

A practical example involves a server managing a batch of incoming files. If a new file arrives at 10:00 AM, it is placed at the head of the queue. The oldest file, 10:00 AM, is processed first, followed by the next oldest, 10:01 AM, and so on. This orderly execution ensures that the system does not become unresponsive or chaotic due to sudden bursts of activity.

The primary advantage of FIFO is its simplicity and fairness. Unlike priority-based systems where a high-priority job might block others, FIFO treats all jobs equally. This makes it ideal for real-time systems where strict timing is critical, such as manufacturing or emergency response scenarios.

Head-of-line blocking occurs when a job arrives after others have already been processed, causing the system to stall. In FIFO, this is prevented because the oldest job is always removed before any new arrival. This eliminates the possibility of a single job blocking the entire system, ensuring continuous operation.

Compared to other policies, FIFO is often preferred for its simplicity and lack of complexity. While priority scheduling can be complex to implement, FIFO requires no special hardware or software modifications. It is particularly effective in environments with limited resources where simplicity is paramount.
